description: Three Indonesian students turning NASA's invisible infrared sky into something everyone can see and hear. Wildan builds the data pipeline and platform. Alif crafts the sonification engine. Nayla leads the science and storytelling. Together, we bridge the gap between raw telescope data and public discovery.
summary: SWARA (Sky Watch with Audio & Real-time Access) is a web tool that makes NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey accessible to everyone, including visually impaired users. Users enter any sky coordinates or pick a point on an interactive all-sky map, and SWARA retrieves real SPHEREx exposures from NASA’s IRSA archive, stacks them into clean frames per visit and detector, and presents them as a blinkable image sequence spanning up to 16 years (WISE 2010-2024 + SPHEREx 2025-2026). Proper motion is measured in arcseconds and cross-checked against the Gaia DR3 catalogue. The 102-band infrared spectrum is turned into sound through scientifically grounded sonification: flux maps to pitch on a pentatonic scale, motion maps to stereo panning, and image structure maps to a field scan, all combined into one composition. Saturated data is flagged with a different timbre, so listeners know when measurements are uncertain. Five curated targets load instantly; any other sky position builds in approximately 90 seconds. Results can be shared via tarot-styled cards with QR codes or direct URL links. SWARA is live, open source (AGPL-3.0), and requires no login.
details:
SWARA (Sky Watch with Audio & Real-time Access) lets anyone pick a spot in the sky, watch it change over sixteen years, and find out what the object is, by eye or by ear. It is built on NASA's SPHEREx and WISE data, and it is free and open to the public with no login and no install.

Try it: https://swara.space/

· Start with Barnard's Star: open it here

· Source code: github.com/wildanniam/SWARA-NASA

The problem

Since 2025, NASA's SPHEREx has mapped the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colors. The data is open, but it is not yet open to everyone. Infrared light is invisible to the human eye, the files and archive queries are built for researchers, and space is shared almost only as pictures. So we asked: how can we make the invisible universe accessible to everyone?

What SWARA does

  • Go anywhere in the sky. Type a star name or an RA/Dec, or click any point on SPHEREx's own all-sky map. The five challenge targets open instantly; a new spot is built straight from NASA's archive in about a minute.
  • Watch sixteen years as a little film. 13 to 18 WISE images (2010–2024) flow into 3 or 4 SPHEREx visits (2025–2026), aligned on the same patch of sky, so a nearby star visibly walks across the field.
  • Measure it honestly. SWARA measures the shift at every visit and prints it next to the catalog value. Barnard's Star moved 9.9″ north in one year in SPHEREx (catalog about 10.4″ per year). When something cannot be measured, the app says so.
  • Hear its light. Each SPHEREx exposure lands on a different wavelength, so one spot gives a 0.75–5 µm spectrum. SWARA plays it as sound: wavelength becomes time, brightness becomes pitch.
  • Look closer. A telescope lens with 6′, 3′ or 2′ fields, a difference image (now minus the first visit), Gaia DR3 stars placed where they were on the image's date, saturated and bad pixels flagged per visit, six color "looks", and a guided tour for first-time visitors.
  • Share it. Every place has its own link, and each object gets shareable cards drawn from its real data: its motion, its light, and its place in the sky.

How it works

  1. Pick a spot. A name is resolved through CDS Sesame (SIMBAD) and moved to its 2026 position with its proper motion. RA/Dec or a click on the map works too.
  2. Gather. SPHEREx Level 2 images are found through IRSA's Simple Image Access service (about 300 exposures for one spot), WISE images come from unWISE through WiseView, and Gaia DR3 stars come from the ESA Gaia Archive.
  3. Combine. Dozens of exposures become one clean median image per detector per visit, across 6 detectors from 0.75 to 5 µm.
  4. Measure. Centroids at every visit give the motion. Aperture photometry with a background ring gives the spectrum. Every number is checked against catalogs.
  5. See and hear. The browser blinks the frames like a film and turns the spectrum into sound.

Under the hood. SWARA reads pixels straight from NASA's public SPHEREx bucket on AWS with HTTP byte-range requests: 5 requests and about 1.25 MB per exposure, instead of about 360 requests and 10.7 MB through a general FITS reader. From Indonesia, that brought a brand-new location down to about one to one and a half minutes. The sound mapping is deterministic: pitch = 110 Hz × 2^(3 · flux / top) on a pentatonic scale, with a clean tone for good pixels and a rougher tone for flagged ones.

Tested on the challenge targets

  • Barnard's Star: 9.9″ north in one year with SPHEREx (catalog about 10.4″/yr), and 142.7″ from 2010 to 2024 in WISE (catalog 142.5″).
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.8″ east and 4.0″ south in about 16 months, with 347 clean spectrum points. This is our main example for listening.
  • RW Aurigae: no motion. Its 4–5 µm brightness drops between visits, but most of its points are flagged as saturated, so we treat that with caution.
  • WISE 0855−0714: WISE shows it moving, but in SPHEREx it is not separated from a background star, and Gaia confirms that star. We say so instead of claiming a detection.
  • R Draconis: too bright. It saturates the detector, so there is no valid measurement, and the app says that.
  • Beyond the list: Wolf 359 measured 3.9″ west and 2.4″ south in 381 days (catalog 4.0″ and 2.8″); Teegarden's Star 5.2″ in 12 months (catalog 5.1″/yr).

Benefits and intended impact

  • From expert files to a one-minute experience. A student, a teacher or a museum visitor can explore real SPHEREx data in a browser, with no install, no login and no FITS files.
  • Science that stays honest. Every number sits next to its catalog value, and limits are written plainly. SWARA is a doorway to NASA's archive, not a replacement for IRSA's tools.
  • A second way in through sound. We designed the sound with low-vision users in mind. We have not tested it with blind or low-vision users yet; that is our next step.
  • Ready for new data. New SPHEREx releases are added through one setting, and the all-sky map address is read from a manifest.
  • Open source under AGPL-3.0, so others can study, reuse and improve it.

What makes it creative

  • Two missions, one story. WISE shows how an object moves (Act 1); SPHEREx shows its light (Act 2).
  • It feels like a real telescope. One continuous zoom runs from SPHEREx's full-sky map down to a single star, using real coordinates and real images, with no invented stars.
  • Science you can hear and share. A spectrum becomes a melody, and tarot-inspired cards turn a star's measured data into something people want to pass on.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, HTML/CSS, and WebGL shaders.
  • Data pipeline and API: Astropy, NumPy, Pillow, HTTPX, fsspec, aiohttp, FastAPI and Uvicorn, managed with uv.
  • Web app: React and Vite, Canvas 2D, WebGL, the Web Audio API, @hscmap/healpix and driver.js.
  • Hosting: Vercel for the web app, and a small Linux server that runs the API.
  • Hardware: our own laptops; no special hardware.
  • AI: AI coding assistants helped write and test code under the team's direction. The idea, product direction and decisions are the team's.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty over hype. SPHEREx pixels are 6.15″, so a few arcseconds of motion is about one pixel. We show the tolerance, flag saturation, and never call a result a discovery.
  • Speed from far away. NASA's archive is in the US and we are in Indonesia, about 260 ms per round trip. That pushed us to byte-range reads and progressive loading: the WISE history starts playing within seconds while SPHEREx data is still arriving.
  • Reliability. The archive search sometimes returns errors for hours. SWARA retries with backoff and tells the user plainly when NASA's archive is not answering. The five examples are static files, so they work even if our API is down.
  • Ease of use. A guided tour, plain-language labels, and links that open one place directly.
  • Data limits. SPHEREx has only 3 or 4 visits per spot so far, which is why we added 14 years of WISE images.
